utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So accused Beara is not here. I understand he's not feeling well. I just want to make sure, Mr. Ostojic, that the waiver is on its way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, Mr. Beara is not feeling well, and the waiver is on the way or should be here this morning. I do have one other request for the Chamber, if I may, through Mr. Beara. He's been complaining, Your Honour, the last two weeks that it's very cold in the cell where they keep him between the sessions, and he's actually even worn sweaters and caps, and we did defer that to the Security Unit and their management team, and they were kind enough to direct our concerns to the general management services. But it's very cold in that cell, and he's actually, for the last four or five days, increasingly gotten sick because of that. So if there's anything the Chamber can do to assist us, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you could block or copy and paste this part of the transcript and have it communicated to Mr. Holthuis, the Registrar, for his investigation and action. Thank you. I'm glad Mr. Beara didn't get the cold from me. The other accused are here. The Defence teams, I notice only the absence of Mr. Meek. The Prosecution team is as it was before, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. The four Defence experts are present. Mr. McCloskey, since we will be starting with the first cross-examination today, has the representative of the US government been made aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, Mr. President, she was planning on being here right after the first break, though I said that may be a little optimistic, but that is when she will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, there are no further preliminaries, I take it. Mr. Ostojic, take my word, we'll act on your complaint and we'll see what can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, could you bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A very good morning to you, Mr. Butler, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey will be concluding his examination-in-chief this morning, and then we'll start with the first of the cross-examinations. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to take us now back in the chronology to around 13 July and talk a bit about Zvornik. And in your narratives over the years, you've cited many documents and logs and reports from the Zvornik Brigade. Can you tell us, just in general terms, when you were going through the material retrieved from that search of the Zvornik Brigade that you talked about, generally what were you on the lookout for, what sorts of information and documents were you on the lookout for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, gravitating back to the purposes behind my analysis of this in the first instance, and having an idea of what the crime base was as a result of the investigation, you know, the first goal that we were doing in examining the military documents was to first gain a fundamental understanding of the organisation of the Zvornik Brigade, where it was on the ground, try and create a day-by-day chronology of what each of the units were doing, and to determine what lengths, if any, there were on the basis of the documents that would link units of the Zvornik Brigade to the actual known crime bases at the time. Where such linkage could be established, the next part was to try and determine the individuals who were in charge of those formations, either commanders or deputy commanders, as a first point for the investigators to then go back out to these individuals and try and determine issues with respect to investigating their potential criminal liability for those acts. So, again, it keeps in part with the two-track origins of my narrative, that -- that same type of research.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 904, and it should be -- we can start with page 1 just so everyone can see where we are.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Binder 6, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, 6, and it should be tab 1. This is a vehicle log for an Opel Accord, and it's for July. And if we could go to page 2 both in the English and the B/C/S, and this is a document you've cited before in your narrative. Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In reviewing the logs of the vehicles that were part of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, this particular vehicle stood out because of the locations that had been identified that the vehicle travelled to, keeping in mind the fuel was a rationed item and that mileage was generally accounted for. You know, when you look at the destinations of this vehicle and how they correspond to, you know, some of the known crime scenes, this particular document, in fact, stands out, particularly its travel on the 13th, 14th, 15th and 16th, even the 17th as far as, so -- so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just blow that up on the 13th so everyone gets a good view of it in both languages, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Staying with our chronology, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you look at the 13th, for instance, it notes: "Standard, IKM, Zvornik local," continuing on, Orahovac on a number of cases and down to Bratunac and then back to Zvornik. This corresponds, particularly the Orahovac notations, to a known crime scene, which would raise the question investigatively why this vehicle is going to that location at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Did you review the IKM log?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, just briefly, did that fit in in your analysis in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. As we subsequently established from cross-indexing the names of these individuals to the military rosters of the Zvornik Brigade and established that these individuals are military police officers and, further, that this vehicle is normally associated with the use of the security branch of the brigade, and then we have, in the IKM log of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, a notation that Drago Nikolic, the chief of security of the brigade, was at the IKM on 13 July, where he had duty at the forward command post. So you can see -- and how when we started putting the connection together with respect to the documents we're showing this, that at some point in time this particular vehicle was used to go to the IKM and then returned, you know, leading us to the next question, you know: Did this vehicle go and pick up Drago Nikolic, particularly with the fact of the notation that Drago Nikolic was extraordinarily relieved from his duties at the IKM at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next exhibit, 65 ter 289. And this -- probably show the first page of that, 289, which is "Delivery Book." But if we could go to page 8 in the English and 116 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, this isn't on my list. Is it? 289.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This one is on the list, according to my boss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move, and in the meantime please check further, Mr. Haynes. Go ahead, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, is this a document that you've cited in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have. I've cited it in both versions of my narrative, and it's a document that I had originally attributed as probably belonging to a vehicle that was responsible for food deliveries. Subsequently, in reviewing the document once again many years after the original review, and looking at it, I now conclude that it's not for a particular vehicle, but what I believe it is is it's a wider dispatch log that would have been maintained at the headquarters, accounting for where vehicles are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you change your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that would be sometime last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does that change your fundamental analysis at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, within respect for what I use this document, I use this document as an indicator that at a point in time, on the late evening of 13 July, because the next notation starts the 14th, that there was a police presence at Orahovac. So regardless of whether this is an individual vehicle log or whether it is a dispatch book, as I now believe it is, it doesn't change the context of the information that I'm gaining from it, which is a police presence at Orahovac at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in the English translation, where we see "Orahovac police," it says "illegible," and could you make anything out in the original, yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the original, I believe that their first number is a zero and then the second number is a 1, so in my analysis of that, what I believe is that, you know, there was a police presence at Orahovac as early as 0100 hours on 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It just says "police." What kind of police do you think it is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the inference that I make in this context is "military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there are other documents that indicate, for example, the military police roster for July of 1995. When you cross-index those names -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. McCloskey and everyone else. We have a small problem. But let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you cross-index the names of military police officers and where they are located on various days, there's a notation on that military police roster that has been altered that reflects a number of military police from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade's Police Company that were at Orahovac on 14 July. So that's where I draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's then go to that roster, and it should be 65 ter -- excuse me, 65 ter 354. It's -- the listing of the names begins on page 3 in the English, and it should be the same page in the B/C/S. With the ERN last 6610, page 3 of e-court is what I'm told, so we need to keep flipping. There's the -- thank you, I think you've got it. And the B/C/S is really the document I think all of us can use, so we can bump the English out of there. That's -- if we could go back to the handwritten. There you go. Thank you. Is this what you're talking about, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "altered," can you explain what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can. When we were going through the documents, as part of our original sorting and catalogue process, and we came across this document. In an examination of the original document we could note that there were clear erasure marks with respect to locations of select individuals on this list from the 14th and the 15th of July, not only on the names, but at the back of the roster, where there was a handwritten index as to what each specific symbol meant, we could clearly see handwritten erasure notations for Orahovac and Rocevic. At the time that we initially had this document, we recognised that Orahovac was a crime base. The investigation did not recognise at the time that Rocevic was also a crime base. That was a scene that we were completely unaware of, because we had no survivors at the time. Knowing that the document had apparently been altered before it came into our possession, the investigation then had the document sent out, I believe, to Dutch forensics laboratory for an analysis of that to confirm our views whether or not what we were looking at was, in fact, valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I can see on your revised narrative on this point, on page 66, you've listed the names of 10 military policemen from that log and noted who was changed to zero and from zero to "T," or from -- to "R." Do you recall what "T" meant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "T" is the general euphemism or symbol that they will use for deployed on the train. Effectively means that they are not in their normal duty location, per se, but in fact have been deployed out on a combat location. So when we see the phrase "T," it's a reflection of the fact that they're not performing their normal duties, that they're out somewhere on -- in the field, is what we would call it, in the United States. And, again, these dates correspond with the dates of deployments of the military police that we have from other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to object to this line of questions by my colleague. I gave him some time and I wanted to know where he was going with this line of questioning. Now it is clear that what he is trying to get from this witness is an analysis of the investigation that was conducted. The witness uses the terms such as "we were looking for." He clearly states that he was looking for evidence, and he is analysing different sources of evidence, which has nothing to do with any military expertise whatsoever. Looking specifically at this document, which deals with the roster, this is not the right witness to come and give us evidence on this roster. Initially, our colleague had proposed an expert witness to come and speak about this roster and manipulation of roster. We haven't heard about this witness. This witness has not been called. Mr. Butler is not the right witness to come and tell us that he saw manipulations of a roster, that he saw presence of military police in a certain location, that this has to do with a crime base. Basically, Mr. Butler is doing what Mr. McCloskey said yesterday, connecting the dots, and this is not the object of his testimony. His testimony, he's there and supposed to help the Trial Chamber, assist the Trial Chamber with some kind of technical expertise. All he's doing is testifying as an investigator and establishing links between different sources of evidence. We believe, Mr. President, that this is completely inadequate, this is not -- improper for him to embark on such a line of questioning. I waited some time, I gave him some leeway, but now we look at the kind of question and it's clear that it has nothing to do with military expertise, nothing to do with the expertise of the witness. It is simply trying to do your job in your place, Mr. President, respectfully put. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would reiterate my argument yesterday that Mr. Butler, as an intelligence expert of many years, has already testified that part of his job as an intelligence expert, which is part of what -- the reason that he was employed and asked to do the job he's done, was to evaluate the credibility and authenticity of the documents that he is reviewing and his ability to look into things like alterations, of course, is crucial to his ability to speak of the documents and the people and the ranks and the units that are on them. Frankly, if he would not have spoken about that, he would have been completely open up, on cross-examination, for looking at documents and analysing them without paying attention to whether they were altered or not. So this is, in my view, a critical part of his analysis, as an intelligence officer, firstly, and as an intelligence officer that is an expert in this case testifying based on his experience as an intelligence officer and now analyst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this goes back to the dilemma we've been having since the beginning of the testimony of Mr. Butler, and even before, when we filed our objective -- our objections, sorry, as to what type of expert is he, or is he an expert at all. We found many objections in this regard, and now we listen to this testimony. This morning, my objection goes much further than the fact that he talks about alterations of the document. An intelligence analyst or someone who works in the intelligence branch, he testified to the contents -- to the nature of the job. But the nature of the job of an intelligence analyst, he looks at facts in order to know what is coming ahead. Now, looking at facts to determine what happened in the past, as an investigator, is not the job of an analyst. And, in any event, he is not here to testify as an analyst, he is not here to testify to establish links between sources of evidence. He is here to testify about the organisation of the Zvornik Brigade, the structure of the Zvornik Brigade, and how this may have affected. If he wants to say -- testify that this is right or wrong, based on the organisation and the doctrine of the VRS and the way it was used at the time, that's different, but now he is solely testifying as an investigator. And because he is a so-called expert, we are allowing him to go further than the other investigators and to make speculation and conclusions. For example, if you look a little further up in the transcript, he uses words as, "I conclude that there were people present there," "I conclude that this was altered," "I conclude ..." All these conclusions are not conclusions saying this is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: ... Militarily speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should be stopped. I can't respond to a continuing argument like this. This is about the fourth time the same argument's been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish, because you are inviting more interjections. Have you finished, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We believe that the conclusions of this gentleman that we have before us are not what he is here for. He is supposed to testify about the structure and to give technical expertise to the Trial Chamber. He's going way beyond that, and we believe that it is improper at this time, and we ask you to stop this, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There was Madame Fauveau before you, Mr. Ostojic, and I also notice Mr. Haynes, if he's still interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was only going to say that I think Mr. Butler probably ought to leave if this is going to go on much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to take much longer. Madame Fauveau, please be brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with what my colleague has just said. I believe it's quite incredible, unbelievable, that on Monday we all came here to listen to an expert witness, but for about a week now we've been listening to the conclusions of the Prosecution submitted through a so-called witness, who is not a witness but a member of the Office of the Prosecution. And the witness has just submitted the arguments of the Prosecution. Today's the fifth day of his testimony, and we suddenly hear that he's not a military expert, that he's an expert in intelligence analysis. I believe that the Defence should have been notified in advance of the actual nature of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We join, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And we join as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I'm not surprised. So Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler has testified almost identically in two previous trials and before the Appellate Chamber. His reports echo the testimony. This is -- there's more notice on the style and content of Mr. Butler's expertise and testimony than perhaps any other witness in this Tribunal, and the counsel had plenty of notice to hone their attack prior to Mr. Butler taking the witness stand on these points. And, frankly, they tried and they lost, and he's been already testifying, connecting the dots like he's done before, and providing his expertise for some four days. It's too late to change course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's close it here. Mr. Bourgon, please, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my colleague has just admitted and conceded that the witness is here only to connect the dots, which is improper. My colleague keeps running the same argument, which is the SALT principle, same as last trial. As early as our pre-trial brief, we said to the Trial Chamber we have to stop this, Mr. President. This is not the same trial, and the Trial Chamber can make its own rulings based on what is announced. This is not a military expert in what he is testifying to today. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are unanimous in our decision. Judge Prost will be explaining it or state our decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: We are agreement with the position of the Defence that there are certainly limitations on the areas of expertise of the witness. For example, general discussion of alteration of documents is not a matter which falls within his area of expertise. However, at the same time, we do agree with the position of the Prosecution, that if in the course of analysing documents for the purposes of his testimony, the witness has formed the view, in his opinion, the documents were altered, it was certainly his obligation, in fact, to relate that position, that opinion, to the Trial Chamber for the Trial Chamber's consideration, obviously. Insofar, however, that the Defence appear to be suggesting that other matters on which he has been testifying to in this particular segment were not within his area of expertise, we do not agree, and in particular with the question and answer to which Mr. Bourgon's original objection was made, because if you take a look at the question and answer on page 9, lines 14 to 25, where the witness discusses the symbol "T" within the document, as well as the correspondence of that with deployment dates of the military police, we are of the view that that is precisely the areas that he is here to provide the Trial Chamber with assistance on. And that is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prost. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was done in that area, anyway. We do have that original log, if the Court would like to see it. It's a very simple thing to look at, if you're at all interested. And let's briefly go to 65 ter 677.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is -- Mr. Butler, briefly, is this a copy of the hand -- the erasure report that you made reference to in your testimony and in your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to skip ahead a bit to try to save some time, because many of these documents you've cited in your narrative have already been mentioned by other witnesses, and I don't think we need to discuss them. So let me skip through many of these engineering documents that are on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For the record, I would just like to note that this particular document that the witness referred to is not a document that has been admitted in evidence and has not been submitted nor discussed before this Court at any time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe the name of the expert has been on the witness list, and we have an agreement with six of seven of Defence counsel that this report would come in. We've been continuing to speak with Ms. Nikolic on that point to try to save our time from bringing in this person to come in and tell us that he sees erasure marks on certain things. Perhaps Mr. Bourgon is not a part of that, but that is the history of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's leave it for the time being, but the comments of Mr. Bourgon enters into the record. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get to an intercept now, Mr. Butler. It should be on your tab 10. It's 65 ter 1164A, and that's the English. D is the B/C/S. And this is from the 14th of July now, and this is at 2102 hours, and it's the Palma duty officer, Major Jokic, Badem, X and Y. And we can read it. We see: "Hello, Badem. Let me talk to Beara." And then B says: "Who wants to talk to him?" Who do you take this B to mean, this answer: "Who wants to talk to him?"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take this to be the switchboard operator who is -- the switchboards are manned constantly, and at this point it's just a question of, you know, the operator basically saying, "Okay, who wants to talk to him before I go find him."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The switchboard operator where?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Badem, which would be the headquarters of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then it says: "The Palma duty officer wants to talk to him. Beara is needed urgently, somebody needs him. The higher house urgently needs him, but he has to call me." Okay, then we go down and I think we can read the rest -- some of the rest of it to ourselves. It's a similar discussion for a while, and then at some point Badem says: "Here is Beara, you have him on the line." And then this J says: "Hello?" X says: "Hello." They go on and talk about things that are difficult -- well, I won't comment on them. Then as we go down, we hear J say: "Is that Beara? Jokic here." Who do you think the Jokic is in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be Dragan Jokic, the chief of engineering for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade who, at this point in time, is performing duty as the duty officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Jokic goes on to say: "We were together, Colonel, sir. Number 155 called you and asked you to call him urgently." And then BE apparently can't be heard from the " ...," and then Jokic says again: "Number 155. That's, I mean, the higher house. You go ahead and call them, you have to, so I don't speak like this." Who do you -- what do you -- is your opinion regarding what Jokic means by this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Major Jokic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just object. I think it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please answer the question. If he knows, he knows. I mean, the witness knows that he is not here to speculate. If he can give us his opinion, he will do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Number 155 is a number that is associated with the operations office of the Main Staff. What, in this context, he's talking about is Major Jokic wants Beara to call that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then we can't hear Beara again, and Jokic says: "Yes, hey, we have huge problems over here." Then we can't hear Beara, and Jokic says: "There are big problems with the people, I mean, the parcel." This term "parcel," is that then a sub -- identifying the meaning of that term? Has that been something you've studied as part of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The phrase "parcel," when used alternatively in the intercepts or in the documents, is a euphemism for "people." Depending upon the context of the actual intercept, in many of the intercepts the phrase "parcel" is used in the context of prisoners. In some cases, particularly in the documents, the phrase "parcel" refers to just"people." So, you know, it's their euphemism of talking around that, and you have to actually look at the context of each and every report or intercept that it's in to try and determine, you know, what they're actually talking about with that euphemism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the witness, based on his military expertise, should not be looking to find what "parcel" was used for in these documents, but he should first establish whether "parcel" has any kind of military meaning or military use within the VRS. Then he can comment as to whether this word has been used for a specific purpose in the intercept. But now he is just doing the work of investigator and saying, "What do I conclude, based on all the intercepts, what 'parcels' referred to." Maybe my colleague can ask some questions to the witness, whether he knows that the word "parcel" was used before and used after and used in many respect within the VRS for many purposes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We do agree that the interpretation of the word "parcel," in the context that we've been talking about, is beyond the -- or is out of the parameters of the witness's expertise, so we prefer if no questions are put again along these lines, and we will of course not give any weight to his answer to your question, Mr. McCloskey. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's keep going down the intercept. Jokic says: "Who? Drago is nowhere around. I don't know where the others are all day." Then it continues to make references to 155 and the higher house. I think we'll go to the next exhibit, 65 ter 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is an objection I'm going to raise again. I've already raised it some days ago. I don't think the Prosecutor can continue reading the exhibit without asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought I was going to ask a question, and I decided not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay, no big deal. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So 1166D should be the English. 1166C should be the B/C/S. This is an intercept at 2227 hours, participants General Vilotic and Jokic, the Palma duty officer. Mr. Butler, have you evaluated who this General Vilotic may be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's your interpretation or your conclusion regarding that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, in fact, the correspondent in this case is General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly when we first saw this intercept and recognised the name, we did go back through the variety of VRS material that we had to determine whether or not there was, in fact, a General Vilotic anywhere within the VRS of whom this might be, and the answer was negative. So, you know, given the context of that and the fact that, you know, within the body of the actual intercept itself it identifies the person as a general officer, it's not an assessment by the intercept operator, I conclude that this is General Miletic, not a General Vilotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, that's B/C/S page 2 and 3, as we'll go through this. All right. We can go down and read this to ourself, though there is a reference to: "Where is Obradovic." And as we go down, we can see this is Major Jokic, duty office Palma. Can you tell us if you've made a conclusion regarding who Obradovic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in that first part, particularly given the answer that in the field, what in fact they're referring to is Obrenovic, then-Major Obrenovic, the chief of staff of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is an error in translation, because in B/C/S the name is correctly spelled "Obrenovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I didn't notice that, though there's the possibility that this is the translation of the handwritten version, but I won't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's keep going down, and there's a discussion where Jokic says: "That's right, they promised me some reinforcements, but they're nowhere to be seen, you know." And then V says: "From where?" Jokic says: "Well, the blues." V says: "Well, see, with that Vasic, fuck him, everything available should be gathered. You must raise them all. Jokic, sound the alert down there in the town." What's your view of who the blues are and the Vasic they're referring to here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "Vasic" in this case is Dragan Vasic, the head of the CSB. The blues are police forces of the Zvornik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need to go to page 3 of the B/C/S, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go down to the bottom. Jokic says: "Obrenovic is really engaged to the hilt ... We are all engaged to the hilt, believe me ... This package really did for us ... We've been reporting about the number of people since this morning, so ... So there." And: "All right, don't me that." "All right." "All right. Do we understand each other?" Jokic says: "Yes." V says: "Go to Vasic there, get in touch with Tripkovic ...," and it goes on. Can you made any analysis about the comment that Jokic makes about: "Obrenovic is really engaged to the hilt ... We all are," and following, what do you -- what can you conclude, if anything, that refers to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, given the engagements that are going on in the Zvornik Brigade at the time and the fact that there are various military units who had been assembled the day prior and who are out in ambush positions, and that the people out in those ambush positions are being led by Major Obrenovic, the context of this conversation deals with issues primarily related to the attack and the ongoing combat with the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Primarily. Is there some other issue that you can conclude about or -- don't speculate.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only other issue that is occurring at the time, is particularly at the time that this intercept is timed, at this time with respect to the crime base you have the prisoners who are being held at Orahovac. Their executions were still being completed and they were being buried, and you still had prisoners being detained at the school at Petkovci and the school at Rocevic, and prisoners were being brought to the school in Pilica. So that's another -- with respect to what was happening at that point in time, that would have been occupying the efforts of the command and the staff. So those are your two major situations that are occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the witness cannot make a conclusion, a single conclusion, he can conclude anything, because we're falling back to speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's precisely what he was asked not to do, if you read Mr. McCloskey's question. And, in any case, we are in a position, if we think that his conclusion is -- borders on speculation, we'll not give it any weight. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we be in closed session, Mr. President, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, let's continue in the chronology to 65 ter 326 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be your tab 12. It's a 14 July regular combat report from the Zvornik Brigade. 326. It's just the first page that I'm interested in. This is in the name of Chief of Staff Major Dragan Jokic. It has a time of about 1840 hours on it. And I just want to refer you to the -- this document briefly. Does it give us an indication of combat activities that are occurring between the column and the Zvornik Brigade at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time -- and just a quick correction. It's actually signed by Chief of Staff -- or in the name of Chief of Staff Major Obrenovic, not Jokic, as you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at this point in time, it doesn't discuss, with the exception of one notation about a large column routed at Velja Glava, most of the report details with the steps that they are continuing to take. So most of this is not detailing the actual combat with the column. It's, in fact, detailing the preventative measures that the brigade is still trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just to take you to that -- the second page of your -- where you corrected me, we see some initials above the chief of staff. Who do you think those initials are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "DJ," particularly given the fact that we know Major Jokic is the duty officer that day, would be his initials, "Dragan Josic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any idea who "MB" is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 327. This has a -- this is much later. It has a "sent" notation at the bottom of it at 011 hours on 15 July, again under the name Chief of Staff Major Dragan Jokic, to the Command of the Drina Corps. I said "Jokic" again. I'm sorry, "Obrenovic." Quit looking at those initials. We see the same initials again. Tell us about what this is, briefly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular time, the column has broken through all of the initial ambush positions and defence lines that had been established in a hasty matter on the Snagovo and the southern part of the Zvornik Brigade areas of responsibility. Colonel -- or Major Obrenovic at this time is informing his superior command, the Drina Corps that, you know, the size of the column that he notes is over two to three kilometres long and that, you know, in his estimation, it is realistic to expect that they will be making a breakthrough of the defence lines in the area of responsibility of two of his battalions, the 4th and 7th, either later that night or early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document. It's 65 ter 297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we move to the next document, could the -- the witness has said that he doesn't know who the individual with the initials "MB," and we have two intercepts that he doesn't know who that is. I'd like to know from the witness, maybe if he can ask whether he tried to identify that individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who would the -- what position would the "MB" be, in the context of these -- that document? What would that mean, again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be, according to their administrative protocol, those are the initials of the actual person who -- the clerk or the typist who actually put the document together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's get to 65 ter 297. And can you just tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which tab is it on mine, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 14.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, and that's B/C/S 135.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that's on the screen is the first page of what we call the orders book for the Engineer Company of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. It is a book that is maintained by the company command that reflects their orders and duties on any particular day, and it's updated on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in just looking at this, do you connect any of this information to your -- to your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just briefly explain what information, and then we'll just go from there. I don't think we need a big explanation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, this is -- this particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be 15 in the English. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at page 15 when it comes up, what it is is a notation that the company commander of the Engineer Company has an awareness of where major pieces of his equipment are operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think we can go to the next. I'm going to the -- well, let's go to the next. That should be your 15, Mr. Butler, 65 ter 302, and page 1 in the English, page -- let's start off with page 1 in the B/C/S as well. Actually, I apologise. Let's skip that. That's one I want to skip, and I want to go to 65 ter 944; B/C/S 1, English 1. And we can start off with the first page of both so you can just tell us what it is, and then we want to go to page 2 in the B/C/S. That's your tab 16.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I just wanted to make sure I had the correct document. Yes, sir, it's a vehicle log for a TAM 80 truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's the significance of this to your analysis, as briefly as you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a vehicle that we've associated with the 6th Infantry Battalion, based on other vehicle documents and logs, and it shows, particularly with respect to 15 July, there are references "Petkovci, Brana, Petkovci." "Brana," as I understand the Serbo-Croatian language, is "Dam," so it's a reference that this particular vehicle was making at least one trip back and forth between the village of Petkovci and the dam and then returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you -- without any details, did that fit into what you call your crime base analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's make sure whether we are looking at the same page. Oh, yes, the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the second page, B/C/S, if we go to the 15 -- I'm sorry, we need to get -- it's not on the screen, the second page of the B/C/S, and English. Okay, then go to the next page. I apologise. If we can blow that up to see the section for 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Looking at the screen, Mr. Butler, just to make sure, and looking at your original documents, I just want to make sure we've got the right section there so that the Court and everyone can see.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you see there, at 15: "Petkovci, Brana, Petkovci"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. A little difficult on the screen here, but, I do see it, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And number of journeys is six?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, and I'll perhaps be able to save some -- 65 ter 304. This is another work log with the same people's names on it, Topalovic and Josic, but it's another vehicle, it's a TAM 75. And if we go to that particular section for 15 July, Mr. Butler, does that information -- what information do you have, and how does that fit into your analysis? Sorry, we need to keep going on to the next page. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only have those two pages in my --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, we're going to have to come back and find -- find that reference. I apologise. Let's go to 65 ter 1177A, which is another intercept. This is dated 15 July at 0952 hours. It's a short reference. It states: "Colonel Beara was looking for General Zivanovic, but he was not there. He said he was to call him at extension 139." I won't ask you about those two gentlemen anymore, but what about extension 139? What, if anything, did your review indicate about what extension that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents we looked at from the Zvornik Brigade seizure, that included the unit phone lists, extension 139 in the Zvornik Brigade is the phone associated with Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to 65 ter 1178A in the English and 1178C in the B/C/S, and let's begin with page 1 of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S. We now have a transcribed conversation that, by the time count, is 9.54, basically two minutes after the previous one, and the participants are General Zivanovic and Colonel Ljubo Beara. And if we can look at that, I won't read it all out, I'll -- but I want to start with you where, according to the document, Beara says: "You know that day, I informed the commander about it. Furtula didn't send Lukic's intervention platoon." Can you remind us or tell us who you believe Furtula is in the context of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this conversation, I believe Furtula is Major Radomir Furtula, the commander of the Visegrad Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about "Lukic," the reference to Lukic's intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is a reference to the individual Milan Lukic, who was a member of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "that brigade," just to be clear --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visegrad Brigade, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Zivanovic says: "And Lukic is waiting at Blagojevic." And then Beara says: "Lukic is here with me and his driver, and we urged them on that." Where do you believe Beara is at the time of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly, you know, connected with the last conversation, at the time this conversation is occurring, I believe that Colonel Beara is up in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll just -- if we could continue to read down ourselves, makes the comment: "Simply he doesn't give a damn about the commander's order. Well now, that platoon has 60 men." When Beara says "the commander's order," can you make a conclusion who the commander would be in that context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that Colonel Beara is a Main Staff officer, the commander that he would be referring to would be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the discussion goes down a bit, and General Zivanovic says: "I can't order that anymore." And then there's this short: "Uh-huh." And then Zivanovic says: "385." Beara says: "385, that's right." And that is -- Beara asks: "What telephone exchange is 385?" Zivanovic says: "Zlatar and 385." Okay, Can you tell us what you believe 385 and Zlatar to be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Zlatar" is the telephonic code name for the Drina Corps. The extension 385 is one that we've associated with the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this comment that Zivanovic makes before that: "I can't order that anymore," what do you think that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reflection that Colonel Zivanovic is no longer the commander of the Drina Corps, and, as such, he no longer has the right to give these types of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can't order what anymore, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't order unit deployments, can't order people of the corps to change dispositions, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how do you conclude that he's no longer commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base that back on prior -- a prior document that we've talked about, which shows that on the evening of 13 July 1995, that General Krstic assumed command of the Drina Corps and that General Zivanovic was relieved of that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Break time, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is a three-part intercept. It may take five minutes. We can -- however you wish. I usually prefer to take the break right on time, but it might take us five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless there's -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now this conversation began at 0954 hours. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 1179A and B. This is another intercept at 1000 hours, about six minutes later from the time the last one started, and it's -- may we have the B/C/S first page, please. This is noted between Ljubo Beara and General Krstic. How does that fit with the last few lines we just read about 385 and the other information you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean, it dovetails right into what I've indicated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you make any conclusion where General Krstic is at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular juncture, General Krstic is, as far as I'm aware, physically located at the Drina Corps IKM, the forward command post down with respect to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as we look at this, Beara starts out saying: "General Furtula didn't carry out the boss's order." Who do you think "the boss" is in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated before, particularly now that he's speaking to General Krstic, completely eliminating him from, you know, the possibility of being the boss, I think we remain back with the boss being General Mladic, his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Beara says -- or Krstic says: "Listen, he ordered him to take out a tank, not a train." Have you been able to make any -- any clear sense out of that -- out of that comment? And again I don't want you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The next one, Beara says: "But I need 30 men, just like it was ordered." And Krstic says: "Take them from Tasic or Sladojevic. I can't pull anybody out of here for you." What do you believe this reference to Tasic or Sladojevic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, particularly when you go further down in this particular intercept where it notes Nastic and Blagojevic, what I believe is that happened that the intercept operator improperly heard the names. He got them close, but in fact were referring to Major Nastic or Colonel Blagojevic, his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And remind us, I think, who Nastic is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Nastic is the commander of the Milici Light Infantry Brigade. Colonel Blagojevic is the commander of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And: "I can't pull anybody out of here for you." What do you think that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given where General Krstic is and what his activities are engaged in with the Zepa battle front, he's already detached the deployed forces of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade at this point in time to return to Zvornik to deal with the military issue of the column. What he is essentially saying is that "I cannot pull any more forces out from where we are that are engaged in military operations against Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then we see the discussion going on a bit. Krstic responds that it will disturb everything on his axis if he pulls them out. I think that's -- and then there's this comment by Beara: "I need 15 to 30 men with Boban Indjic. I can't do anything." Do you know who Boban Indjic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Boban Indjic is an individual who was a subordinate of Milan Lukic at the Visegrad Brigade. They are associated from their time beginning at the early part of the war from April, May, June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Krstic states that: "Ljubo, this," something, "is not secure." Beara says: "I know, I know." Krstic says: "I'll see what I can do, but it'll disturb a lot. Please, you have down there at Nastic and Blagojevic." Then Beara says: "But I don't have any. If I did, I wouldn't still be asking for the third day." So what does that indicate to you, when he says "the third day"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, you know, going backwards in time, that the purpose why Colonel Beara needed these men was an issue known as early as 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Krstic says: "Check with Blagojevic, take his Red Berets." And you've talked about this subject briefly, but can you just tell us what you think that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Beret is a intervention platoon that's subordinate to the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. There's a prior reference of the units of the Red Beret being sent to Milici for a, quote, "task down there" which we take to be their part of the operation against Zepa. In fact, what other information has developed is that most of the Red Beret Platoon at this particular time left the battlefield and married up with members of the Srebrenica SJB. Many of them were reserve policemen and showed up and wanted to become reserve policemen in Srebrenica rather than remain in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, so we see the next comment by Beara: "They're not there. Only four of them are still there. They took off, fuck 'em, they're not there anymore." Krstic says: "I'll see what I can do." "Check it out and have them go to Drago's." In the context of this conversation now, who do you think he's referring to when he says "go to Drago's"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic at the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then it goes on: "I can't guarantee anything. I'll take steps." That's what Krstic says. And then Beara says: "Krle, I don't know what to do anymore." And then Krstic says: "Ljubo, take those MUP guys from up there." What do you think that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a reference to the various police units that are engaged in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be those police units that are engaged along the road from Kravica, Konjevic Polje. It alternately could be municipal police units from the Zvornik Municipality. It's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then Beara says: "No, they won't do anything. I talked to them. There's no other solution but for those 15 to 30 men with Indjic. They were supposed to arrive on the 13th, but didn't." Is there any other indication of any of -- any Visegrad guys or Indjic guys on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and there is an intercept that refers to the fact that a bus had been sent down to Visegrad to bring individual members up, but that bus had suffered a mechanical breakdown and it had never arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as we go down, it says -- Krstic says: "Ljubo, you have to understand me, you guys fucked me up so much." What do you think that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that, in this particular context where now he's short of troops to engage in the Zepa operation, the fact that more and more soldiers who should be being used in combat operations are being detailed for their involvement with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Beara says: "I understand, but you have to understand me too. Had this been done then, we wouldn't be arguing over it now." Then Krstic says: "Fuck it, now I'll be the one to blame." What's Krstic worried about here, in your view, if you don't speculate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The answer to that question has to be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the Court doesn't want to hear his response, I'm fine to go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can safely go to the next question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you're finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm very close. Mr. President, I would normally ask Mr. Butler his view on the 3,500, what that means, but we have this word "parcels" which was the reference to your earlier ruling. Do you want me to ask him that question or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then we're done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see shakings of heads, so I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have the break, but before we do so, we have an oral decision completely unrelated to what we are dealing with. This is our oral decision on the admissibility of the Borovcanin interview against the co-accused. The Trial Chamber recalls the Appeals Chamber decision on appeals against decision admitting material relating to Borovcanin's questioning of 14th December 2007, in which the Appeals Chamber remanded the issue of the admissibility of the Borovcanin interview with regard to Borovcanin's co-accused to the Trial Chamber. Following the appeals decision and in the circumstances of the case arising therefrom, the Trial Chamber hereby admits the Borovcanin recordings and the Borovcanin transcripts against -- or vis-a-vis the other co-accused. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm slightly puzzled, with respect, by that, because I had assumed, on reading the Appeals Chamber decision, that at the very least, this Trial Chamber would invite further submissions from the parties. That was my understanding of what the Appeals Chamber was saying. They were saying it needed to be remanded, for the matter to be reconsidered on a rather different basis. But if the Appeals -- I beg your pardon. If this Trial Chamber takes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We didn't read it -- we didn't read it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you read the reversal, you will understand why. Thanks. So let's have a 25-minute break, which means let's fix the -- it's 20 -- we'll meet at 10 minutes past, or 8 minutes past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Beara's waiver has arrived and we've seen it. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go to 65 ter 328, page 1 in both languages. And this is a regular combat report from the Command of the Zvornik Brigade. This has the name of Commander Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic on it, with a time stamp of about 1911 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, can you briefly give us a synopsis of what this is communicating and whether you think it accurately reflects the situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is -- sorry. This reflects the knowledge of the VRS and particularly the Zvornik Infantry Brigade of their combat situation during the morning and early afternoon hours in a very general extent, does not get into details, and also lists out the primary tasks of the units with respect to that. Again, it's not a very detailed report, and in the future you'll -- you know, later that day, because it's not a detailed report, you'll see a far more detailed report about the military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when -- near the bottom of -- well, in paragraph 2: "Units which participated in combat activities in Srebrenica and Zepa areas returned during the day to the brigade's area of responsibility and are involved in an action against enemy groups retreating from Srebrenica." Can you outline who you believe that refers to, units and, well, top personnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As both the documents and, I believe, prior testimony reflect, on the early morning hours of 15 July 1995, the two battalion-sized formations of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, under the command at that time of Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, and were engaged in Zepa, were withdrawn from that battlefield and directed to return back to the Zvornik Brigade area to be engaged in military operations against the column. I believe the timing is such that these particular formations were back in the brigade zone by approximately noon on 15 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this just brief reference to brigade area of responsibility, is that at all related to your other previous brief discussion when you talked about brigades' area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 329. This we have as a handwritten document, and on the first page of the English and B/C/S, it is from the Command of the Zvornik Brigade, 15 July, entitled "Interim Combat Report," with a time stamp of 1925 hours on the 15th. Is this related to the reference you just made about more detail?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And referring to the first three big paragraphs, there's -- can you just synopsize that very briefly? I don't want you to repeat that, but is that the situation you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is. It gives a fairly detailed description on what the Zvornik Brigade Command, and in this particular case specifically the commander, understands the enemy situation to be, what impact it's having on his subordinate formations, and what they are doing particularly with respect to what areas of the battlefield they're trying to seal off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'd like to take you now down to the -- I believe it's the fourth paragraph. That should be in the B/C/S page 2, beginning: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain." What do you view this term "as well --" excuse me, the phrase "as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain"; what is your interpretation of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the sentence, Colonel Pandurevic is noting the number of Muslim prisoners held in schools in his brigade zone, and he's reflecting the fact that they are guarding those prisoners, that obligation of security to guard the prisoners. "Restoration of terrain" is the CLSS English translation of the Serbo-Croatian phrase "asanacija." I'm not sure. I detail that in my report. I'm not sure that it's come before the Trial Chamber as to the exact definition, but it's the rough equivalent of the process to bury biological, human, animal waste, things of that nature, in order to prevent a biological hazard from developing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your view that that is a reference of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view is that that is a reference of he's reporting that part of his obligation is to bury the bodies of those individuals who have already been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about "asanacija." Of the battlefield that's resulting -- that we've just seen from the 13th, 14th, 15th of July, in those reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, it's a matter of -- a function of timing and a function of looking at the engineer records, looking at where the column is on the battlefield. In this point in time, where the column is and where the Muslims are taking military casualties, the Zvornik Brigade is not involved in burying Muslim military casualties at that point. That particular area of terrain is still under Muslim control. The only appreciable amount of bodies that they're burying at this point in time have to be the prisoners that were executed at the schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 3017, and this -- this original is -- the date is not clear up in the left-hand corner from the original. Do you -- can you glean a date from this document? Let's -- we should probably wait until we get the English up.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you look at the Serbo-Croatian version, the B/C/S version, you'll notice a time stamp there of 19 July, 1920 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what's the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original version of the B/C/S either -- there seems to be an inordinately large blank between where the "9" should be. I think the most logical explanation is we are looking at a "9" that failed to typed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And why is it you call our -- have you called our attention to this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, this is the first -- at this point in time on 19 July, this is the first document that reflects the fact that pertaining to the larger amount of Muslims who were killed in the column and other battlefield casualties who are laying out on the battlefield, the first time that they are talking about that -- going after and burying these individuals before they start to become a biological hazard. So you have two groups of burial operations, one related to the known crime scenes. Subsequent to that, you have the efforts to conduct the burial of those individuals who were casualties as a result of combat in the column area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 3016. This is a document from the Command of the Drina Corps, from the assistant commander for logistics, Lazar, Colonel Lazar. I believe that's a mis-type. It should be "Acamovic." Is that correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this document is entitled: "Clearing up of the battlefield," or in the B/C/S I think we can see "asanacija." Is this similar to what you just testified about, a similar document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in fact, it outlines specific areas of the battlefield with respect to the Zvornik Brigade with respect to Kamenica and Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 2754. A bit of a different area here for a moment. We have a Main Staff document now, and I don't know if you -- it's to the Krajina Corps and the Drina Corps for information of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, commander or chief of staff personally, from -- it should be on the list under 2518, if people are looking. Chief of staff's representative, I think it's the same -- the boss says it is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: She's right again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe that is just a translation issue. It should be "standing in for the chief of staff, Major General Radivoje Miletic." This is a report on the dispatch of infantry company to assist the 1st Zvornik Brigade, and it -- so we can see it talks about a unit from the 1st Krajina Corps going to assist the Zvornik Brigade. Can you briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to raise an objection with respect to the way the Prosecutor interprets a translation mistake, because I believe that this word can be translated in many different ways, and I would like the Prosecutor to abstain from commenting on the way the function -- the title of General Miletic has been translated in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an old debate. I believe - Ms. Fauveau can correct me if I'm wrong - but the terminology that's used here, [Bosnian spoken], is the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I'll stop you here. I think this matter can be dealt with on cross-examination like you did previously with other witnesses, Madame Fauveau. Let's see if my colleagues disagree with me. Judge Kwon. Okay, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a consistency of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And of course Madame Fauveau will have every right and opportunity to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to -- the problem with Ms. Fauveau here is that there's a French way of interpreting this -- remember this debate, it gets very complex, and I'm not sure cross-examination helps Mr. Butler. But, in any event, I apologise. I'll try -- I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, how does this document that appears to involve a unit from the Krajina going to help out the Zvornik Brigade, how does that fit into your analysis, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this document is a -- a classic example of, you know, where the competence of the Main Staff would be with respect to their authority to order units from a different corps to be resubordinated, or a company or several companies from a different corps formation to be resubordinated to a different corps, in order to deal with a tactical situation. By the 15th of July, the morning hours, the VRS leadership was becoming acutely aware of the developing military crisis in the Zvornik Brigade, and they were actively involved in trying to find additional forces that could be sent to the Zvornik Brigade area to combat the column. Colonel -- or, I'm sorry, General Krstic certainly would not be within his competence to direct a unit from outside his corps to do this. The only organ of the VRS that could do this would be the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that unit arrives to the Zvornik Brigade -- or when that unit arrived to the Zvornik Brigade, under whose command was it under, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When that unit arrived in the Zvornik Brigade zone and was employed, it was under the command of the Zvornik Brigade commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you relate this particular -- did you relate this particular unit to any crime base?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The -- this particular company is -- has been associated with the crime base known as "the Nezuk crime base."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 297. And just to clarify, that Nezuk crime base, that's part of a charge in the indictment, is that correct, referring it, in rough terms, that way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
