utterances.text: Okay. 65 ter 297. Again, this -- and that's page 136 of the B/C/S and page 16 of the English. We see this order book from the engineers that you've referred to before. We see references to a BGH-700 and an ULT-220. Have you incorporated that into your analysis connecting it to a crime base?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you also, in your narrative, noted some logs related to various excavating equipment on similar dates?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next one, which would be 27 in your tab, Mr. Butler, 1187A, 65 ter, and C in the B/C/S, page 1. An intercept, 16 July, at 1111 hours. According to the operators, it's between Colonel Ljubo Beara and Cerovic. Can you remind us who you believe Cerovic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's Colonel Cerovic, who is the assistant commander for morale, legal and religious affairs for the Drina Corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any opinion on where Cerovic was at the time of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Unless I'm mistaken, I believe he's functioning as the duty officer of the Drina Corps at their headquarters in Vlasenica on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You say unless you're mistaken. Well, perhaps -- well, I don't want to go back and show you the duty officer roster at this point, but let me ask you about -- can you remind us who Turkulja is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel Turkulja is the chief of the armoured and mechanised forces. He's a staff officer on the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think we can all read that ourselves, and what I want to ask you is: This conversation about Beara and triage, have you identified any information in your review of the materials that there was some kind of a medical triage done where prisoners were actually looked after in a medical way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only prisoners that I am aware of that were looked at in a medical way would be those prisoners who were initially treated at the Milici Health Centre or subsequently transferred to the Zvornik Hospital, and then after that to the dispensary at the Standard headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. I am not aware of medical treatment being administered to any of the other larger groups of prisoners at any of the schools in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next exhibit, 65 ter 377. This should be the B/C/S page 146, English 27, out of the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook. And I want to ask you, it says -- or the English translation of 03089333, if that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What tab is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be 28 for you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, first of all, this page, it should be ERN 5764 out of the notebook. Do you see the notebook reference, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do, I found it. It was mis-tabbed in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, I didn't. I'll have to go off the screen. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, let's go off the screen. And just taking a look at that page, is that something you've read before and read in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to conclude what date that page is from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at this juncture, we're talking 16 July 1995, although I'd like to see the larger document in context, because there is a -- there is a dating sequence to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you -- just if we can blow that up a little bit -- make a reference to the section at 1115 hours: "It was reported from Zlatar that a triage of wounded and prisoners must be carried out. It was reported to Beara." Now, that previous intercept we looked at was the same -- was 16 July, 1111 hours. Do you relate these two documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe they're directly related.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this -- right below that, it says: "At 1120 hours, Badem, Colonel Jankovic was looking for Major Malinic." Can you tell us who you think that is and where he is, the Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference to Colonel Jankovic and Badem is a reflection of Colonel Jankovic's presence at the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade headquarters. Major Malinic is the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment's Military Police Battalion. It seems to indicate that maybe Major Malinic, you know, may be somewhere up in the Zvornik Brigade zone at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's -- let's go to the next document. It's an intercept, 1189A and C. It should be B/C/S page 2, English page 1. This is the Zlatar duty officer speaking to the Palma duty officer. So as you've stated before, that should be the duty officer of the Drina Corps at Vlasenica speaking to the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade. And in the second line, it says: "Palma duty officer speaking. 500 litres of D2 for Lieutenant Colonel Popovic." "For Lieutenant Colonel Popovic?" Then it goes on, and it appears that a person named Basevic gets on the line. Okay. Can you just tell us who, in this context, you think Popovic is and Basevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this intercept, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic is Vujadin Popovic, the chief of security of the Drina Corps. Major -- the individual named Basevic is Major Basevic, who the chief of technical services for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think we can see ourselves that it's about a discussion related to this 500 litres, and it goes on and says: "500 litres of D2 are urgently being asked for, or else the work he's doing will stop." And then it goes on, as we can read it to ourselves. Basevic says: "Two tonnes are arriving now at your place." There's a reference to: "Well, then get in touch with Rocevic." Do you know what that has anything to do with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then there's a reference to Major Golic. Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Golic is the -- is an intelligence officer. He -- with the Drina Corps. He's subordinate to Colonel Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And according to this, what would be his position? Well: "Give me the operations duty officer." Can you relate that at all to Golic or not, or is that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe on this day that Major Golic is the -- is the duty officer this day. I think it's, in the context, it's a separate question, once they get back to the duty officer, the question is Major Golic there by chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then Palma says: "Golic, Pop just called me and told me to contact you. 500 litres of D2 have to be sent to him immediately. Otherwise, his work will stop." Then they go down a little bit, keep reading, and then: "A bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica village. That's it." "500 litres." Now, in your view, where is this D2 supposed to go to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It directly references the village of Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is the second reference that: "Popovic needs the fuel. Otherwise, his work will stop." Are you aware of any -- any work that is going on in the area of Pilica that would require these kinds of amounts of fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be related to the transport of Muslims being held at the school to the Branjevo Farm, where they're subsequently executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other construction or movement, transport, or anything else in that area, besides that fact you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, there's no corresponding combat activity or any other activity of the nature that would call for that fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 291. It should be just a one-page document, some kind of a form. I note, in the left-hand corner as we look at the original, we see a date of 16 July. The name and address of sender is: "Military post 7469, Zvornik." Name and address of recipient: "Commander of the Drina Corps, addressee station," in parentheses: "For Lieutenant Colonel Popovic." Then in the body of it, there's a reference as we can see related to diesel fuel, up to and including number 1, and then it -- by the order -- according to the order of Captain S. Milosevic: "Remark, out of 500 litres of D2, 140 litres were returned." What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typical logistical invoice, if you will, reflecting the fact that on a given day, a product or a certain commodity was dispersed. We see these types of documents with reflection to all manner of technical goods; ammunition, batteries, fuel, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see also down in the left-hand corner a date that's handwritten in: "17 July 1995". Then we go over and we see M. Krstic as a special service organ -- under "special service organ," excuse me, and then: "Findings and signature of commission to be received by ..." And then: " ... Received by Bogicevic, Branko." Now, can you relate this document to the previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What you're seeing in this particular document is the end result of a process, and I've discussed this in my narrative, whereas the -- you know, the chief of security, you know, acting within the field of his competence, does not have the authority to order the Zvornik Brigade to disperse fuel. What has to happen is it has to be turned into a request through the branches of the Drina Corps, through the rear services, for approval, and then be back down. And I think what you have between that particular prior intercept and this particular document is a fair illustration of how that process worked, from the requirements of Colonel Popovic, up through the security chain and operational chain to the Drina Corps, across to the logistics and technical services people, and then back down again to the logistical people of the Zvornik Brigade, who then now have the proper authority to disperse the fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your knowledge, who is in command of the Drina Corps -- of the Zvornik Brigade on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about on the 15th of July, after he returned from the Zepa operations, who was in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to clarify, Colonel Pandurevic was never not in command of the Zvornik Brigade. Even when he was down dealing with issues related to Srebrenica and Zepa, there was no formal relinquishment of command. The fact is that in the absence of Colonel Pandurevic, you know, the chief of staff, Major Obrenovic, had the authority and in fact dealt with the day-to-day operations of the brigade. But there's not a question of at some point in time, either before or after, there was a formal relinquishment of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you outline for us what the military responsibilities are for a brigade commander that's out of his zone, you know, leading his units in another operation, in relation to his command that you've just referred to, the command of the Zvornik Brigade in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to the doctrinal issue of how the JNA defines "command," there is a formal process by which if it is going to be a situation where the brigade commander is going to be out of his zone of operations for an extended period of time, where his deputy or another officer, if that may be the case, will be appointed as standing in for the commander, it's a legal delegation because it does recognise that even though the chief of staff, functioning as the deputy commander in his absence, you know, can deal with most day-to-day issues, there are some legal or other administrative issues that even the deputy commander cannot accomplish on his own and needs -- and needs to have a formal order that he is in fact standing in for the commander. You see this illustration in August of 1995, when Colonel Pandurevic does take two -- a battalion or two battalions from the Zvornik Brigade and is deployed to the battle front in the Krajina, where this formal designation takes place. Back to Srebrenica, you do not have a formal relinquishing of the responsibility of the command, so in that context, while Major Obrenovic, as the chief of staff, is controlling day-to-day operations and is responsible for the conduct of those day-to-day operations, Colonel Pandurevic, as the brigade commander, still remains overall responsible as the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, getting back to our fuel and -- issue, did you review the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook for any potential reference to this fuel situation on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to 65 ter number 377. It should be page 148 in the B/C/S and 29 in the English, or 0308933 in the English translation. Blow that up a bit. Do you see anything on that page that you have -- has been part of your opinion on this topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, the second bullet point is a reflection of the past two exhibits that we've been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 1199A. This is an intercept. The B/C/S is in B. This is from 16 July, at 1912 hours, and we have a Basevic. Is that the same Basevic, in your view, that you've referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And he says: "Well, the petrol's run out completely. Miki, I said to Miletic today, when I was on the phone with him, like, to do with this request that -- that Zvornik sent, and Sekovici." "Zvornik is solved." "I said I have no petrol, oil and --" "Listen, Zvornik is solved." "Well, I know, I saw ... You know, but the problem is what's going on across Sekovici this way ..." And they talk about, as we can read, something related to Sekovici and 600 litres. Do you have any idea who Miki is in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the reference to Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the context, I believe, that the individual they're referring to is General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that Colonel Basevic -- or, I'm sorry, at that time Major Basevic is calling -- as the Drina Corps technical services officer is relaying the message up to the Main Staff that they're out of fuel with respect to what they can provide to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you relate -- does this -- do you tie this in at all in any way with this fuel situation regarding Popovic and Pilica that we discussed earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Correspondent Y is reflecting that Zvornik is solved, so in the context of what we've discussed earlier, my view is the fact that whoever correspondent Y is is responding to the fact that the fuel has been delivered to the Zvornik Brigade or that the Zvornik Brigade's requirement for the use of fuel is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The objection is rather late. That was a terrible leading question, but it's been answered. But in the broader sense, Mr. Butler's presence is entirely ancillary to this process. I completely accept that he's entitled to express his view, his credentials having been laid out, as to what the effect of my client is when he departed with Tactical Group 1, and that's a matter about which I will cross-examine him. But the rest of the examination for the last 20 minutes has barely involved a question of him and has merely involved Mr. McCloskey reading out verbatim document after document after document and inviting Mr. Butler to say whether there is a link between them, which Mr. McCloskey seeks him to make. It involves not an ounce of expertise. It is a form of Prosecution submission. That's all it is. And I make the objection at this point, and I invite you to stop it now. This is really just a Prosecution closing speech, saying, "This document links to this document links to this document." It doesn't need Mr. Butler to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Ms. Fauveau, and then you answer everyone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully support what my colleague just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Likewise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I join the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is practically the identical objection that we've been hearing all along, I believe first in the motion that was filed challenging Mr. Butler's expertise. Mr. Butler, I believe, is assisting us to identify who people are, where units are, as he just did, the policy of command as it relates to when Vinko Pandurevic came back, who would have been in command of the Krajina unit, who would have been in command of the situation where his officers are dealing with fuel. These are all key military issues. Some are -- yes, they're simple when looked in isolation, but they're not simple when looked at the massive amount of documents and material and facts that can only be truly interpreted by one with a military background, with a knowledge of the JNA and a knowledge of the Zvornik Brigade. This may appear simple, but it is rather complex, and the job of the security officer and the intelligence officer is a difficult one, and it is not something that is suggested by Defence, and we have specifically asked Mr. Butler, over the years, to be our expert in this very difficult field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I confer with my colleagues, let me hear you first, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I'm afraid Mr. McCloskey, in my submission, misreads your decision. Your decision set out the ambit, unlike in the Krstic case and the Blagojevic case, of Mr. Butler's expertise. He was not to come before this Tribunal as, as it were, a second counsel for the Prosecution. He was to come before this Tribunal with an expertise which you identified. And I'll leave that point to one side. The questions, other than the one which I concede he was perfectly entitled to answer about, the effect of my client going and fighting in Srebrenica, that he has been asked in the last 20 minutes have been so trite that they have been an insult to all of our intelligences, and in particular yours. To ask this man, "Who do you think the Popovic is," in that intercept, and then to ask him again, "Who do you think the Popovic is that is referred to in the duty officer's notebook," five minutes later, is an insult to all our intelligences, and it's a device, really, to make this submission to you through this witness. You are not assisted by this, to use the phrase that has been repeated in many of the judgements about the use of Prosecution investigators as witnesses and so-called analyst experts, you really are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd just like to add one comment to this, Mr. President, and the fact that this witness -- one of the things that has been discussed before in the case law of this Tribunal is whether it was possible for a witness to present summarising evidence. In this case, it is not even summarising evidence, it is selective evidence and the result of an investigation. This is what is wrong with it. It will make your work difficult, and it will make our cross-examination twice as long. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps Mr. Zivanovic would agree with me that the name "Popovic" is one of the most common names in Bosnia, and I don't ask that question over and over again to insult anyone. But on a document that is so significant for Mr. Popovic, for the Prosecution, for all of us here, I take the line of conservativeness and I ask Mr. Butler, because he's the one that looks at these lists of all the Popovics and their various jobs. And I don't know if the Defence of another Popovic is going to be here or not, but that's why I ask those questions. Mr. Butler is uniquely able to tell this Court which officers from this army could be possibly placed here. And I must say this is about the eighth objection on this identical point. You have carved out a few situations where you don't want me asking questions. I believe I got your message on that, and I am trying my best to do that. But asking basic questions about who are in an intercept and the background and tying the details is what Mr. Butler has been doing for four days. It's way too late in the game to suggest to any attorney that's been up here doing just this for four days, for the fifth time to make the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps without realising, you put several issues on our plate to deal with. We draw certain distinctions between some of the information that is being sought from the witness and other. For example, we definitely agree with the Defence objections, that questions like the last one that you put to the witness, namely, comparing or contrasting the two documents you referred him to, whether correspondent Y is responding to the fact that the fuel has been delivered to the Zvornik Brigade and that the Zvornik Brigade requirement for the use of fuel is completed, we don't believe that that is the kind of question you should putting to the witness. These are matters that can be deduced from the face of the document itself, and you should restrict your questions to those instances when it's not clear from the document itself, at least for us it shouldn't and can't be clear, and that a clear picture can emerge only if there is the expert opinion of the witness forthcoming. Having said that, we then disagree completely with what has been objected to by the Defence in relation to the identification of individuals. Where it is clear from the document itself who the individual is, I think you shouldn't -- we think you shouldn't put the question. But this is one reason why the witness has been admitted as an expert witness, because sometimes the identification of persons indicated in a document by a military expert is perhaps the best way of helping us identify those individuals. So we don't look at certain questions as an insult to anybody's intelligence. At times, they are useful. We'll stop you any time we think that a question is uncalled for, unsolicited, or which does not fall within the parameters of the expertise of the witness. Otherwise, please try to avoid having the witness confirm what appears on documents, which is clear for all of us to read and draw conclusions from, without the need of any expertise. I hope we made ourselves clear. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And that was absolutely my understanding of your previous rulings as well, and I am -- I am trying to do that. It's -- and I will of course continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It really depends on how many objections we get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but come on, I mean, it's been -- I've been counting. We've had over an hour -- over 60 minutes of objections in the space of one week, and that is not beyond what was to be expected. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's very hard to tell, Mr. President. It reminds me of the old joke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are wasting more time. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Butler, let's go to 65 ter 1195A. This is an intercept from the CSB -- or, excuse me, by the CSB. It's a conversation from about 1615 hours on the 16th of a conversation between Main Staff duty officer and General Mladic, and General Mladic was not audible. Can you briefly describe what this is talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular intercept is talking about the indications that the Main Staff is receiving that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic has taken the action to effect a battlefield truce with the Muslims in the column and has authorised them to proceed to Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's a mention of the president in here. How does that fit in, and Karisik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in the context of my earlier testimony about the fact that the military is not the only reporting mechanism from these areas, the police and the security services have their own reporting, it's a reflection of the fact that while the military may not have mentioned something, that the information pertaining to this battlefield truce is possessed by the highest levels of the RS government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And his notation: "I asked the duty officer to urgently connect me with him ..." What's that a reference to? Or actually, as we look down it says: "Now I'm waiting for them to call me because Pandurevic hasn't called for the last four ..."?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean they're looking for a -- they're looking for the explanation of the brigade commander as to whether or not this particular event has taken place, and if it has, why. They owe -- they owe the president an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And have you identified documents on the same subject that help flush it out a bit more in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have, and those are reflective of the interim combat report for 16 July 1995 which details that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's -- let's go to another document of the duty officer note -- the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook, 65 ter number 377, page 30 in the English, B/C/S page 149, reminding ourselves that the last intercept was at 1615 hours. There's a notation here, if we could blow up the part -- particularly the second half: "At 1620 hours, message from Zlatar that one officer from the command was to go immediately to the commander and send a written report on the current situation, the agreement and arrangements made with the other side. Immediately sent to Mijatovic." How does that relate to the previous intercept, if at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it corresponds. Again this is a reflection of what activity is taking place in Zvornik on the basis of that prior intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is Mijatovic, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a Lieutenant Mijatovic who is a Zvornik Brigade officer. I believe he may be duty officer this day or may be just an -- functioning as an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, then the next comment: "Message from Zlatar that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic must go to Vinko Pandurevic in the field at 1640 hours." Is that related?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, as a senior-ranking Drina Corps officer who happens to be in the Zvornik Brigade zone at that period, this is a reflection of now Zlatar, the Drina Corps Command wants him personally to go to talk to Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says: "Message through the 1st Battalion that Popovic must report to the duty officer so he can be sent on a task by Zlatar." Can you remind us where the zone of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The 1st Battalion zone is the northernmost zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and within that zone you have Pilica village and you have the Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 1201A and 1201C. This is an intercept of 16 July, Palma, Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic and Rasic. Do you know who Rasic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rasic is identified in the document as someone on the phone from the Operations Centre. My memory has failed a little bit on that one, I couldn't tell you off the bat whether he's actually a member of the Drina Corps operations staff or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. "Lieutenant Colonel Popovic was asked to be connected with General Krstic at Zlatar, and he was not there. He asked to be connected with the OC." Now, we can read this, that it starts out with: "Hello, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic speaking." "Rasic here, can I help you?" "Rale!" And Popovic says: "I was just up there." "Yes." "I was with the boss personally." "Yes." "Here where I am -- you know where I am?" "I know." "Well, you got his interim report." "All of it." "It's just like he wrote it ... It was there on the spot" -- sorry, "I was there on the spot and saw for myself he had received some numbers ..." What, in your view, is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, he's referring first to the interim report that Colonel Pandurevic has written, and, second, he's noting, "I was with the boss, personally," that he in fact spoke to Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have a conclusion about, when he says "received numbers," what that has to do with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that in the context of what we're discussing, Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Popovic is referring to the large number of individuals in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how about the next part, the part that says: "I'll come there tomorrow so tell the general ... I've finished the job." "You finished?" "I finished everything." "Good." What do you believe that's a reference to, if you can, without speculating?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this -- in this context I believe what we're discussing now is Lieutenant Colonel Popovic's involvement in the execution of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go -- let's go down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appears in the context of this sentence, where you have: "Well, that's not important, I will come there tomorrow, so tell the general ..." And then you have a blank space, and then you have: "I finished the job." You read the subsequent sentences: "You finished?" "I finished everything." Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, from what he is doing in the Zvornik Brigade area, his past association with the job of the executions, he's not involved with an operational job with respect to combat or assisting Colonel Pandurevic or the Zvornik Brigade in combat. So when -- I take that break, and in conjunction with the next couple of sentences, you know, I believe that Colonel Popovic is talking about the job that he was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At 2116 hours, were the executions continuing, as far as the evidence that you've reviewed reflecting up in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the state of the execution is by this point in time the executions were all completed at the school facilities or at the large-scale holding facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then I want to continue on. Popovic mentions: "I'll come there tomorrow and I'm sure that's all been taken care of, you know." "Good." "After I bring a transport from there." "Right." "Well, in general, there weren't any major problems. But up there, there were horrible problems, and that thing the commander sent was just the right thing." What do you think he's talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, and I've commented on this particular intercept before, first in the Krstic case, and again I've changed my opinion of what that particular phrase is, based on prior information from, I guess in this case, it's Protected Witness 168, that what they're talking about in this particular context, as to the "up there," refers to the situation on the ground at Baljkovica, where the column has passed through and where the Serbs -- the Bosnian Serb Army in that area has suffered a large number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and we'll get into that change of view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but one moment, because that doesn't explain the phrase from that sentence, "and that thing the commander sent."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The phrase "what the commander sent," and again I go over this in my written report, is that in that particular context, we're talking about the series of military reinforcements that the commander or, by extension, the Main Staff has been sending in to the zone of the Zvornik Brigade. That thing that the commander sent, I interpret to be the various military units that have come up from Bratunac, that have come from the Krajina Corps, that have come from other locations, as well as police units that have been detailed in, are the requisite military reinforcements that Colonel Pandurevic needed in an attempt to stabilise the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then as we go on, it talks about: "Just the thing ... Horrible ... It was horrible." Again, is that a reference -- what's that a reference to, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's a reflection of the conflict with the column and the subsequent Serbian casualties with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which were roughly how many?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall the number of the deaths from the various battalions that are attributed to combat on that day, I believe the number is in excess of 40 casualties or 40 deaths that day, and I think I've seen numbers as high as 120 wounded with respect to combat in that particular location. A very intensive combat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And relative to your knowledge of the rest of the war, how -- you know, how intensive or perhaps -- of course in the idea of the VRS, how horrible was that and compared to other -- other sorts of combat casualties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may stand to be corrected on this, because there may have been events elsewhere, but I'm not aware of a single incident where the VRS and in particular one unit of brigade size had 40 combat deaths in such a short amount of time, in less than a 24-hour period. So this is an issue of significant gravity for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you incorporate that knowledge into your viewpoint that you've just told the Court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, not -- not even necessarily my knowledge, but in the subsequent 18 July report that Colonel Pandurevic sends to the Drina Corps, where he outlines all of these very issues as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let me go on. Then after that, Rasic says: "Listen, Vujadin." "What?" "Tell me, did anything arrive there now from Vidoje Blagojevic?" "From Vidoje? "Today." "Yes. You mean manpower?" He says: "Yes, yes. Did anything arrive? Something was supposed to arrive." "Yes, it arrived. It's up there, it's up there, but it didn't arrive on time and it wasn't brought in on time. And the others who did arrive -- did arrive, but they were late, and so they weren't brought in on time, and that's why the commander who was there had problems." "When exactly did Blagojevic's men arrive?" Okay. You've mentioned just now that you had changed your analysis from the Krstic trial on this previous part of the intercept. Does that include the part that I just read?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what your first -- your Krstic analysis of this section was? And let's -- we best go, well, line for line.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I had indicated before on the issue of units, during the initial stages of the Krstic trial, the information that we had at hand -- that I had at hand reflected the use of members of the Bratunac Brigade or men from Bratunac with respect to their use in a crime base, crime scene; in fact, Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you remind us what witness provided that information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That witness, I believe, was Drazen Erdemovic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. In the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Subsequently as the investigation continued to work on and additional material came forward, I came to recognise that what we were in fact discussing was not an issue of the sending of Colonel Blagojevic's people to the Branjevo execution site, but in fact the sending of a company that had been requested from the Bratunac Brigade as part of the military reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you set out that view to the Appellate Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. Once I made that determination that I had misinterpreted this particular passage or had attributed initially an erroneous interpretation to it, I did in fact make that known and I did testify to that extent for the Krstic Appellate Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more? We want to know whether you are going to finish today. You need to finish today, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that we're all very tired, but I would like, nevertheless, to draw your attention to page 72, line 18 to 24 of the transcript. The witness has just said that he changed his mind regarding -- or on the basis of the information provided by PW-168. Hereby, the witness admits and acknowledges the way he proceeded to reach his conclusions. Since his testimony is not based on his technical knowledge but on specific information he derived from the investigation conducted by the Prosecution, I would like you to decide that this witness should not be treated as an expert witness, but as a fact witness, as an investigator from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I, of course, have faith that the Chamber will treat this witness however you see fit, as according to your prior rulings, but I think it's very fair for Mr. Butler to talk to an officer (redacted) and get his perspective on how horrible it was to see the casualties that they had at Baljkovica to help him interpret documents. Here, it was absolutely essential. And I think it's absolutely fair. You can imagine how much affect it had on the case of General Krstic, perhaps 10 years' worth, so this is the kind of information that's absolutely critical for this Court to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to support the information provided by my colleague, but also to highlight the fact that this is -- the point that she's making is not what Mr. McCloskey responded to right away. The issue is that all of the testimony of this witness is based on investigative work, investigative work which is one-sided and which makes him not an expert but a fact witness, as an investigator, and that his testimony should be treated in this respect. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't you both think that this can eventually form part -- take the form of a submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed it will, Mr. President, and we will also be raising it in cross-examination, but my colleague decided to raise it at this time because we have then made a number of objections and it is our feeling that my colleague from the Prosecution is not abiding by the rulings of the Trial Chamber with respect to the questions that he can and cannot ask. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would join to this objection and to add that Mr. Butler did not spoke just with the (redacted), that this is the Witness 168, (redacted), and it is not mentioned by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position, common position, unanimous, in fact, is as follows: We are professional Judges, as we keep repeating here, and we are not professional Judges with inverted commas, we are professional Judges, and we have taken note of your submission, Madame Fauveau, and also take notice of the other Defence counsel that joined with your submission. We feel we have no problem at all in identifying when the witness is testifying as a military expert and when maybe he has gone beyond his expertise evidence and testified on other issues. We have given direction, in the course of these five days, to the Prosecution, given direction as to what kind of questions ought and ought not to be put, and that was in the presence of the witness himself. At the end of the day, we have no doubt at all in our mind that we'll be able to make our own assessment. Having said that, I think we can bring the witness back in. And are you going to finish, Mr. McCloskey? I see that the US representative is no longer here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I have not spoken to her. I hope to finish. I've cut quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, again, I hate to be mis-trustworthy on this issue, but most of the big issues, I think, we're -- or the trickier issues, we're through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, she is here. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we go to 1202C and D, 65 ter number. It should be 36 in your tab, Mr. Butler, and we're still on that last issue, one last area, one last intercept related to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. In this short intercept, we actually see a reference to -- it's dated, actually -- sorry, it's timed the same time as the previous intercept. If we can recall in the previous intercept -- then don't broadcast again. I see the problem Mr. Bourgon had spotted earlier. Just to remind us that in the previous intercept, they're asking us when Blagojevic's men got back, and R said: "Okay. Find out exactly and call me back." And he says: "I will." And now we see a reference to Vidoje Blagojevic at 1705 hours, 30 men came from Doboj and 1725 hours, 100 men came from Banja Luka. Now, in the testimony in Krstic, what time did Drazen Erdemovic say the men from Bratunac arrived, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be approximately 1300 hours on 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did this -- did you -- were you aware of this intercept when you'd made your first interpretation of the previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was not. I don't recall being aware of this intercept. The intercept project remained a work in process while we were doing the actual trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did this intercept play any role in your changing your mind and deciding that the men that arrived late were not from Blagojevic, as you'd talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 1204A and C. We're still on 16 July. We're now getting later. It's 2233 hours. We have X is Strbic. Let's go to B/C/S page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we're doing that, just for your information, we are redacting part of your last latest intervention, Mr. Zivanovic. You'll find out why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this intercept, we see: "Hello, Palma. Put Drago Nikolic or Strbic on the line." Do you have an opinion who this Strbic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two individuals. One is Lieutenant Strbic who is a member of the rear services staff of the Zvornik Brigade, and one is a Lieutenant Milorad Trbic, who is the assistant security officer for the Zvornik Brigade. Given the context of the conversation and the fact that he's asked for Drago Nikolic first, and because we have other correlating information that Lieutenant Trbic is the duty officer on this day, I believe that the individual here is Lieutenant Trbic, not Strbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And down in the middle of this, it says -- the question from X to who you say is Trbic: "Was Popovic over at your place?" And Trbic says: "Yes. He was here and gone." "Where did he go?" I think we can read the rest of that ourselves, and I won't ask any questions about that. Now, we're going to be skipping some things, Mr. Butler, so I'll try to keep up with you on the tabs. Okay, let's go to 1218A and 1218B, another intercept. Now we've switched to 17 July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I fail to see -- the last intercept that we went through, there was an identification of maybe someone called "Strbic" who might be called "Trbic," but there were no questions on the intercept, and I don't see why this intercept was used. I waited until to see the next one, to see if there was a correlation between the two, but my colleague should not bring up intercepts just to identify a name, without telling us what -- where it comes in the analysis made by the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to sort out what I think you want analysis on and what I think you don't want analysis on. I looked at that. It was pretty clear that these guys were looking for Popovic, and so I left it sit. And that's what I did. But I needed to bring out who that was, who the duty officer was, so you can all evaluate this later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see no problem, Mr. McCloskey. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 1218A and 1218B, on the 17th of July --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have a tab number for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, that's tab 45. All right, now, if we look at this, it's basically a general is looking for Popovic and wants him to report to the IKM. What do you -- what can you make, if anything, of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at this juncture General Krstic is not at the main command post, he is at the forward command post. I believe it's located in the town or village of Krivace, and this is an intercept reflecting the fact that Zlatar 1, which is often referred to -- you know, Zlatar 1 personally is the code name that's given to the commander of a various unit. Zlatar 01 is often referred to as the corps commander. Palma 01 will be personally the commander of the brat -- sorry, the Zvornik Brigade. So in this context where it says who wants to know, Zlatar 01, I mean, we're talking directly about General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see here that he's asking Golic to find him and have him report, so let's go to the next intercept, 1219A and B. It's a 17 July intercept, and it's 1244 hours, two minutes later. It's between X and Trbic, and Trbic says: "Yes, can I help you?" "Tell me, is Pop there?" "No." "Do you know where he is?" "Well, he went to that -- he went towards that task." X says: "North of you?" "Yes." Briefly, what do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of what was happening in the Zvornik Brigade at the time, the "task north" doesn't refer to military activity, it refers to the work continuing to bury the bodies of those who had been executed at the Branjevo Farm. The other military documents and records we have reflect that the actual installation of the mass grave there didn't take place on the 16th, at the time they were executed, it in fact occurred the next day, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, it goes on to say: "Get in touch with him, please." And then Trbic says: "But it's very hard for me to do that." X says: "I know it is, Drago told me, but don't think of it that way." "Please try to get in touch with him." Any idea who X is in that context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can make an educated guess who it is, based on the context, but I don't have a distinct identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, let's not guess. Let's go to the next one, 1220A and 1220B. And this is -- again, it's a few minutes later, and it says: "Hello!" Hey, Trbic!" Yes?" "Listen." "Yes!" "It's changed again." "Yes." "You get in touch with him, let him finish that work." "Yes." "So let him finish that work that he's doing and have him report immediately here at Golac's." Do you know what "Golac's" is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe in this context we're talking to a Golac, which would identify the location that X is at at the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Okay, let's go to the next conversation, 17 July, 1224A, 1224C. At 1622 hours now, and it's Popovic and Y, and Popovic says: "Hello, it's Popovic ... Boss ... Everything's okay, that job is done ... Everything's okay ... Everything's been brought to an end, no problems ... I am here at the base ... Can I just take a little break, take a little break, take a shower, and then I'll think again later ... Basically, that all gets an A ... An A ... The grade is an A. Everything's okay ... That's it, bye, take care." When he says, "I'm at the base," do you have a conclusion where that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I take that to be at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when he says, "Hello, it's Popovic, boss," do you have a view who that would be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, I take that it's Popovic's boss, which would be General Major Krstic, the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, because of prior intercepts which relate to the fact that the boss or Zlatar 01 is looking for a report from Popovic, in part just because the tone of the conversation appears to be differential to a superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next intercept, which is 1234A and C. Actually, I think that's self-explanatory, so let's skip it. Let's go to 65 ter 336, and this is a 19 July 1995 Command of the Zvornik Brigade. It's a regular combat report. And do you relate this to your investigation and your narration -- your narrative study?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly, how so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, going back to paragraph 2, it does in fact identify which company of the Krajina Corps, in this case out of the 16th Krajina Brigade, came from the Krajina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade area. It also identifies other units that were from outside the brigade zone that have now gone to the Zvornik Brigade. So, I mean, I use that one as a way of keeping track of which particular units have been sent from various other areas into the zone of the Zvornik Brigade to be engaged in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And anything about the rest of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It also reflects one comment: "During the search operation, two Muslim soldiers were killed and 13 were eliminated." In context with the known crime base, this particular notation reflects a very close parallel to the actual crime that occurred with respect to what is known as the Nezuk execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think -- let me just correct your reading of that, "two Muslim soldiers were captured"--

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- "and 13 eliminated."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if Mr. Butler ought to be invited to say whether he reconsiders that assessment, now he's re-read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Butler, do you wish to add anything, having --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, just a simple reading error on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go to 65 ter 405. We're now, I think, going back in time briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But can you just tell us why you've cited us to this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, part of the analytical process of corroborating which units have come in and where they have gone, this particular document is just another reflection of which particular unit of the 16th Krajina Motorised Brigade has been sent to the zone of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to your tab 54, 65 ter 340, and this is an interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade in the name of Commander Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. And want to refer you to the third paragraph, as I think people can read the context of that from what's on there: "We request from the Corps Command that the Exchange Commission start work as soon as possible. We also require instructions as what to do with the prisoners, where to put them, and to whom we should hand them over." Now, you have made reference to this before. What is your analysis of that -- of that statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. While in a number of combat reports the issue of small numbers of prisoners of war have been reported up the chain of command, this is the first piece of -- or first document that I am aware of, in the context of the time, where somebody within not only the Zvornik Brigade but the Drina Corps proper is requesting guidance with respect to what about prisoners who we might want to exchange, and this is already 22 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion on whether a brigade commander normally needs to ask about whether or not prisoners -- what to do with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material with respect to the Zvornik Brigade, and many of these have been exhibits that we've discussed with respect to the Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, Drina Corps, reflect prior policies or reflect past policies pertaining to the procedures of handling prisoners of war and everything of that nature. So, in theory, he shouldn't have had to ask for specific guidance. It should have been continuing as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll try to save some time here. Have you reviewed two documents from the Main Staff, one is 65 ter 41, just for the record, and one is 42. They are in your tabs 55 and 56, relating to five tonnes of diesel coming to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you -- what's your view about the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fuel dispersed -- that fuel dispersal and the fact -- who it's under the control of is reflective of the fact that that fuel is to be used for what is known investigatively as the operation to dig up the primary graves of the mass executions in the Zvornik Brigade and to then remove the remains to secondary locations. At this point in time, the International Community is already well aware of the fact that large executions have occurred, there's been photographic evidence of that brought before the United Nations, so this represents the effort and the fuel used in order to dig up those remains and remove them to what are commonly referred to as the secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 836. This is taking us to a Bratunac Brigade report. It's entitled: "Report on meetings of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade." I would refer you, that should be in your tab 57, to English page 11, B/C/S page 24. And under a note: "The working meeting of the commander, with commander staff and battalion commanders," 16 October 1995, under "Nikolic" there's a comment: "We are currently engaged in tasks issued by the Army of Republika Srpska General Staff." It probably says "Glavnica," "sanitation," which in the original is in parentheses "asanacija." First of all, who do you think Nikolic is and secondly, what do you think this is a reference to, this "asanacija"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First part of the question, the Nikolic in question is Captain First Class Momir Nikolic, the chief of security for the Bratunac Brigade. The second part of the question, I believe this is also related to activities on the digging up of the primary graves in the zone of the Bratunac Brigade and the taking of the remains in those primary graves to what are known as the secondary sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could skip ahead to 72, 65 ter 1880, and --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which tab would that be for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a tab 72. I'll have to look at it off the screen. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It will be there. And I'll ask you, while we're waiting: Did your report include a brief section on some prisoners that were taken in Milici, treated in the Milici Hospital, and sent up towards Zvornik? And we don't need any details on that, but did your report include that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at this exhibit, 65 ter 1880, was that something that you discussed in relation to those patients?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in looking at -- near the bottom of it, we see a notation: "18 wounded enemy soldiers," or "18 wounded enemy have undergone surgery and have been transferred to the hospital in Zvornik on the orders of the Main Staff." Do you relate this particular document with those Milici patients that you talked about in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 1499. This is a map, and I won't spend very much time on it. This is the last exhibit, 65 ter -- actually, we did find the exhibit that we had messed up a bit before, 65 ter, it's now 304. It's that TAM 75 truck from the Petkovci Battalion. And if we could just hit that and we'll be able to finish on time, I'm sure. I was hoping we would -- well, this is fine. Mr. Butler, is this map something that you've had a chance to review?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know what collection it came from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it came from the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you -- in your review of these maps, is this -- can you tell, is this got any -- is it an operational map, or what is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be, to some respect, an operational map. There are notations on it pertaining to the Srebrenica enclave. The lines that are outlined in yellow are -- reflect movements of the Bratunac Brigade. Looking where these arrows are and everything else, they do not reflect the axes of advances for the actual operation Krivaja 1995. What they reflect are these movements of at least the Bratunac Brigade sweep operation-wise in the post-combat phase, after -- after 12 July, 13 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Aside from those dates that we see that reflect the Srebrenica operation and the Zepa operation, were you able to date this map at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, from that point, I mean, the notations on the Srebrenica side appear to be dated, like I said, 12 or 13 July. Even though it's dated 12, the actual marks on the graphic showing where units are deploying is indicative of that date. And I believe further down, scrolling on the map, there's another date listing as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But aside from those dates, any way for you to determine when this map was actually created?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may very well be that there are two separate times that this map was annotated. It could also have been part of it was done before, part of it was done after. There's another date reflection that notes 27 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go to the Exhibit 304, the TAM -- the TAM truck. You've already discussed I believe it was a TAM 80. Do you recall, Mr. Butler, at this point whether you had discussed a TAM 75 from the same unit in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if it was another TAM 75 or a TAM 80, but I am aware that there were two identified vehicles or trucks from the 6th Battalion that were noted to have been making these trips back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to page 2 on both of those, please. And I think we can blow up the B/C/S version, especially in the area of 15 July. Do you see your reference that -- or what you referenced in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Butler. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Next week we'll have -- we'll start with the cross-examinations, and so your presence, I think, will be required. I thank you for having been with us today. Mr. Bourgon -- I think the witness can leave the courtroom. We'll see you again on Monday morning, Mr. Butler. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to take this opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence counsel for the various accused in this case, we've already met a couple of times to try and discuss who would take what part of the testimony of the witness with respect to cross-examination to avoid any overlap, so we will -- again, we are planning to meet this weekend to further establish our respective positions. However, I wish to say that as far as I'm concerned, my estimate -- my initial estimate of four hours is likely to be drawn out to more rather than less, based on the nature of the testimony of the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We avoided asking you for a revised estimate precisely because it may be appropriate to allow you the weekend to think about the witness's testimony and to regulate yourselves accordingly, but we'll talk about it on Monday. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I would just simply say that the Prosecution objects to over two weeks of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So have a nice weekend. We'll meet again on Monday morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
